newsitem.title: USA: Lawmakers, White House ready for new budget talks.
newsitem.headline: Lawmakers, White House ready for new budget talks.

text.p: Congressional Republicans Wednesday wrapped up internal discussions on tax and spending cuts and prepared for intensive negotiations with the White House on legislation to balance the budget by 2002.

Despite days of meetings, House and Senate Republicans could not bridge their differences on a number of politically touchy items including a Senate-passed plan for a 20-cents-per-pack increase in the federal cigarette tax.
"We don't have to (decide) right now and my position certainly is the House has got real heartburn over a cigarette tax," said Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican.
House leaders fear they will not have the votes to pass long-sought tax-cutting legislation if the cigarette levy is included.
Republicans also remained divided over proposals to increase Medicare premiums for the well off and cuts in Medicaid payments to hospitals that serve the indigent.
In many areas where the Republicans came to closure, they moved to the right.

That could complicate talks with the White House and make it tough to meet an Aug. 1 target for passing tax and spending legislation. The bills are needed to implement a five-year budget deal between the White House and Congress.
The new Republican tax plan amounts to a net $89 billion tax cut over five years, slightly more than the budget deal called for, a congressional aide said.

Republicans kept a House proposal to index capital gains for inflation which has drawn a veto threat from President Clinton. They decided to provide a $500 per-child tax credit to fewer low-income workers than the White House wants.

Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle said the good news was Republicans were ready to bargain on taxes. "The bad news is they produced a bill that only Republicans can support. So now negotiations must begin in earnest," he told reporters.

Republicans have decided to give states broad grants to design and run their own children's health programmes, providing either insurance or services. The White House wants a more tightly defined programme.
The budget deal included $16 billion to provide care to as many as half the nation's 10 million uninsured children.
The deal calls for about $115 billion in Medicare cuts and $15 billion in Medicaid reductions over five years.

Speaking to reporters, White House spokesman Mike McCurry scrupulously avoided criticising the Republican tax compromise, saying only: "They clearly did not write the final version of tax legislation last night."
Asked if Clinton would veto the bill as worked out by the Republicans, he said: "The bill's a long way from finished."

Budget efforts have been complicated by the disagreements between House and Senate Republicans and by the abortive coup launched by some House Republicans earlier this month to oust their leader, House Speaker Newt Gingrich.
Gingrich, trying to get Republicans to focus on passing the budget, Wednesday said Republicans must put the "tiresome and overwrought" saga over his leadership behind them.

The effort to balance the budget has been helped by the U.S. economy's strong growth, which has produced unexpectedly high tax revenues and shrunk the deficit to $11 billion for the first nine months of the fiscal year, which ends Sept. 30.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said Wednesday it would be a "very good year" for the federal budget deficit but that no final estimate was available yet for the end of fiscal 1997.
